references.text: The entire pericope ([ref:Luk 20:1-8|Luke 20:1-8]) provides the context for this answer: the high priests and scribes' question about Jesus' authority, and his counter-question regarding John's baptism, which they dared not answer.

The parallel passage in [ref:Matt 21:25-27|Matthew 21:25-27] recounts the same event where the chief priests and elders replied that they did not know where John's baptism was from, because they feared the consequences of either possible answer.
The parallel passage in [ref:Mark 11:33|Mark 11:33] tells the same story: they answered Jesus that they did not know, and Jesus then refused to answer their question about his authority.

In [ref:Luk 20:5-6|Luke 20:5-6], their dilemma is explained: If they said "from heaven", Jesus would ask why they did not believe him; if they said "from men", the people would stone them. Therefore, they chose to say that they did not know.

In [ref:Joh 9:21|John 9:21], the parents of the man born blind use a similar evasive strategy by saying "we do not know" to avoid consequences, just as the chief priests here answer that they do not know.

In [ref:Jer 38:14-15|Jeremiah 38:14-15], we see an example of leaders unwilling to listen to the truth even when it is presented to them—a parallel to the religious leaders' reluctance to acknowledge the truth about John's baptism.

In [ref:Luk 22:67-68|Luke 22:67-68], Jesus himself says that if he tells them, they will not believe, and if he asks, they will not answer—reflecting the same dynamic as this refusal to answer honestly.
